title: NAC vs Milk Thistle: Which Liver Supplement Is Better?
excerpt: NAC vs milk thistle for your liver, hangovers, and fatty liver: how each works, what the research really shows, side effects, and whether you can take them together.
metaDescription: NAC vs milk thistle: how each supports the liver, what the research shows, hangover and fatty liver evidence, side effects, and taking them together.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** NAC and milk thistle are both sold as "liver support," but they work in completely different ways, and neither one has strong evidence behind it for healthy people who drink socially. NAC (N-acetylcysteine) is a building block your liver uses to make glutathione, its main antioxidant. It has one rock-solid medical use: in hospitals it is the standard antidote for Tylenol (acetaminophen) overdose. Milk thistle is a plant extract whose active mix, silymarin, has been studied in liver disease for decades with mixed and mostly disappointing results in the better-quality trials. If you are choosing between them for general liver support around drinking, NAC has the clearer biological story and milk thistle has the longer track record of being gentle and cheap. Neither is a reason to drink more, and neither has good evidence for preventing hangovers.

**The quick version of the choice:**

- **Pick NAC** if your interest is the glutathione and antioxidant angle, you don't take nitroglycerin or blood thinners, and you can tolerate a supplement that sometimes upsets the stomach and smells of sulfur.
- **Pick milk thistle** if you want the most-studied liver herb, prefer something with a long record of being well tolerated, and don't have a ragweed or daisy-family allergy or diabetes medication to worry about.
- **Pick neither** if what you really want is to feel better the morning after. Neither one has good human evidence for hangovers. The things that work best are still drinking less, pacing, eating, and sleep.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article summarizes general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before starting either supplement if** you have liver disease or have been told your liver enzymes are high, you take prescription medication (especially blood thinners, nitroglycerin or other nitrates, diabetes medicine, or drugs your doctor monitors with blood levels), you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or you have asthma. **Get medical care right away** if you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pain under your right ribs, or confusion. If you think someone took too much acetaminophen, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) or 911. A supplement is never a substitute for emergency care.

## NAC vs Milk Thistle at a Glance

| | NAC (N-acetylcysteine) | Milk thistle (silymarin) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A modified form of the amino acid cysteine | An extract from the seeds of the *Silybum marianum* plant |
| Main idea | Supplies cysteine so the liver can make more glutathione | A mix of plant compounds (mainly silybin) thought to act as antioxidants and to stabilize liver cell membranes |
| Strongest evidence | IV and oral NAC are the standard hospital treatment for acetaminophen overdose | IV silibinin has been used in Europe for death cap mushroom poisoning |
| Evidence in alcohol-related liver disease | Mixed; one notable trial in severe alcoholic hepatitis showed a short-term benefit only, alongside steroids | Mixed; a Cochrane review found no clear effect on deaths in the higher-quality trials |
| Evidence for hangovers | No good human evidence; animal and lab studies on acetaldehyde only | No good human evidence |
| Typical supplement dose | 600 to 1,200 mg a day | Around 140 mg of silymarin two or three times a day (product labels vary) |
| Common side effects | Nausea, stomach upset, diarrhea, sulfur smell | Mild stomach upset, bloating, loose stools |
| Watch out for | Nitroglycerin, blood thinners, asthma (mainly with inhaled forms) | Ragweed and daisy-family allergies, diabetes medicine, hormone-sensitive conditions |
| Cost | Low to moderate | Low |

## What NAC Actually Does in Your Liver

To understand NAC, you need to know about **glutathione**. Glutathione is a small molecule your cells make from three amino acids: glutamate, glycine, and cysteine. It is one of the body's main defenses against reactive, damaging molecules. Your liver uses it constantly to neutralize by-products from breaking down drugs, alcohol, and normal metabolism.

Of those three building blocks, cysteine is usually the one in shortest supply. That makes it the bottleneck. NAC is a form of cysteine with a small chemical tag (an acetyl group) that makes it more stable and easier to take as a pill. Once absorbed, the body strips the tag off and uses the cysteine to make glutathione.

### The acetaminophen story is the reason NAC is famous

When you take acetaminophen (the drug in Tylenol), a small slice of each dose is turned into a toxic by-product called NAPQI. Glutathione latches onto NAPQI and neutralizes it. In an overdose, NAPQI piles up faster than glutathione can handle it, and liver cells start to die.

Doctors found in the 1970s that giving NAC refills the liver's glutathione supply fast enough to prevent that damage, especially when it is given within about 8 hours of the overdose. It has been the standard treatment ever since. This is real, well-established medicine.

The catch is that this success often gets stretched into marketing it can't support. Hospital NAC is given in large, carefully timed doses, usually through an IV, to people who are glutathione-depleted from a specific poisoning. A 600 mg capsule taken by a healthy person who had four drinks is a completely different situation. The hospital result tells you NAC can feed glutathione production. It does not tell you that a daily pill protects a healthy liver from alcohol. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the acetaminophen side of this in more detail.

### NAC and alcohol

Alcohol is broken down in two main steps. First it becomes **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound linked to many hangover symptoms and to longer-term damage. Then acetaldehyde is broken down into acetate, which is mostly harmless. Heavy drinking also generates oxidative stress, which can wear down glutathione stores over time.

That gives NAC two theoretical angles:

1. **Restoring glutathione** that heavy drinking may deplete.
2. **Binding acetaldehyde.** Cysteine has a chemical group that can react with acetaldehyde. Older animal studies from the 1970s found that cysteine protected rats from otherwise lethal doses of acetaldehyde, which is where much of the "take NAC before drinking" advice traces back to.

Both ideas are plausible. Neither has been confirmed in good human trials of social drinkers. The closest human evidence comes from a small Finnish trial of **L-cysteine** (a related compound, not NAC) that reported some improvement in hangover symptoms. That is a different supplement, it was a small study, and its results haven't been widely repeated. We cover it in our [L-cysteine for hangovers](/never-hungover/l-cysteine-for-hangover) guide.

In actual liver disease, the most cited trial is a 2011 study in the *New England Journal of Medicine* that gave people with severe alcoholic hepatitis either steroids alone or steroids plus IV NAC. The combination improved survival at one month, but the difference was no longer significant at six months. That's a hospital treatment for a serious illness, not evidence about supplements for social drinkers, but it's a fair summary of NAC's track record: real biological effects, limited proof of lasting benefit.

## What Milk Thistle Actually Does in Your Liver

Milk thistle is a flowering plant whose seeds have been used as a liver remedy for centuries. The extract sold in supplements is called **silymarin**, a mixture of several related plant compounds called flavonolignans. The main active one is **silybin** (also called silibinin).

In lab and animal studies, silymarin does several things that sound useful:

- Acts as an antioxidant and reduces markers of oxidative stress.
- Appears to stabilize the outer membranes of liver cells, which may make it harder for some toxins to get in.
- Reduces inflammation signals.
- In animal studies, slows the scarring process (fibrosis) in some kinds of liver injury.
- Has been reported to help keep glutathione levels up, which is one point where it overlaps with NAC.

### The death cap mushroom exception

Milk thistle's most impressive real-world use is the medical one. In parts of Europe, an IV form of silibinin has been used for years as a treatment for poisoning from the death cap mushroom (*Amanita phalloides*), where it appears to block the toxin from entering liver cells. Like hospital NAC, that is a specific, high-dose, supervised treatment for one poison. It doesn't translate into proof that a capsule protects a healthy liver from alcohol.

### The human evidence in alcohol-related liver disease

This is where milk thistle disappoints. Silymarin has been tested in people with alcohol-related liver disease for decades, with conflicting results:

- An Austrian trial from 1989 in people with cirrhosis reported better survival with silymarin, which drove a lot of early enthusiasm.
- A later Spanish trial in people with alcoholic cirrhosis, published in 1998, found no survival benefit.
- A **Cochrane systematic review** of milk thistle for alcoholic and hepatitis B or C liver disease concluded that the higher-quality trials showed no significant effect on deaths or complications, and that more careful trials were needed.

Part of the problem is that silymarin is poorly absorbed. Only a small fraction of what you swallow reaches the bloodstream. Some brands bind it to phospholipids (sold as "phytosome" forms) to improve absorption, but the evidence that this changes real-world outcomes is limited.

The fair reading: milk thistle is gentle, inexpensive, and biologically interesting, but in people with real liver disease it hasn't shown the clear benefits its reputation suggests. If you'd like to see how milk thistle stacks up against DHM specifically, see our [DHM vs milk thistle comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-milk-thistle-which-liver-supplement-more-effective-2025).

## NAC vs Milk Thistle: Which Is Better for Your Liver?

There is no study that compares NAC and milk thistle head to head for liver health in people who drink. So any honest answer has to piece the evidence together. Here is how they compare on the points that matter.

**Mechanism.** NAC has a more direct and better-understood mechanism. It provides the bottleneck ingredient for glutathione, and we know from the acetaminophen experience that this works when glutathione is actually depleted. Milk thistle's effects are broader and less specific: antioxidant, membrane-stabilizing, anti-inflammatory. Those are reasonable, but they are harder to pin down and harder to prove.

**Evidence in people.** Both have mixed results in liver disease, and neither has convincing evidence in healthy social drinkers. Milk thistle has more total trials, simply because it has been studied for longer. NAC has the stronger single proof point (acetaminophen poisoning), but that's a narrow and very different situation.

**Safety.** Both are generally well tolerated at normal supplement doses. Milk thistle usually causes fewer stomach complaints. NAC has a couple of more meaningful drug interactions to be aware of (see below).

**Who benefits most.** The people most likely to benefit from either are people who are glutathione-depleted or have real liver stress, which is exactly the group that should be under a doctor's care rather than self-treating. For a healthy person who has a few drinks on the weekend, the honest expectation for either supplement is modest at best.

**Our take:** if you want one liver-support supplement and have no conflicting medications, NAC has the clearer reason to exist. If you are sensitive to stomach upset or take a nitrate or blood thinner, milk thistle is the gentler option. Neither should be the main part of your plan. If your drinking is heavy enough that you are worried about your liver, the most effective step is to cut back and ask your doctor for a simple liver blood test.

## NAC vs Milk Thistle for Hangovers

This is probably the real question for many readers, so here is a direct answer: **there is no good evidence that either NAC or milk thistle prevents or treats hangovers in people.**

The theory is stronger for NAC. Because cysteine can react with acetaldehyde and NAC feeds glutathione production, it's at least plausible that taking it around drinking could blunt some of the toxic load. That theory comes from animal and lab work. No well-designed human trial of NAC for hangovers has shown a meaningful benefit. The best related human data is the small L-cysteine trial mentioned above.

Milk thistle has even less to go on. It's a liver supplement in the long-term sense: the idea is that it supports liver cells over time. Hangovers are a short-term mix of dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation, low blood sugar, stomach irritation, and acetaldehyde. There's no reason to expect a few capsules of silymarin to change how you feel the next morning, and no trials showing that it does.

If hangovers are the problem you're trying to solve, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence. Our overview of [glutathione for hangovers](/never-hungover/glutathione-for-hangover) also explains why taking glutathione directly is a less reliable route than supplying its building blocks.

## Can You Take NAC and Milk Thistle Together?

Generally, yes. There is no known dangerous interaction between NAC and milk thistle, and the two are often found together in combination "liver formulas." Their mechanisms overlap a little (both have been linked to glutathione) but are mostly different, so taking both isn't doubling up in the way that taking two painkillers would be.

That said, stacking supplements has some practical costs:

- **More side effects.** Both can upset the stomach. Taking both makes that more likely, especially on an empty stomach.
- **More interactions to track.** Each one has its own medication cautions, and combining them means checking both lists.
- **Harder to tell what's working.** If you start two things at once and feel different, you won't know which one did it.
- **More money for an unproven benefit.** Doubling up doesn't double the evidence.

If you want to try both, a sensible approach is to start one, give it a few weeks, then decide whether adding the second is worth it. If you take any prescription medicine, show your pharmacist the labels of both. Our [DHM supplement stack guide](/never-hungover/dhm-supplement-stack-guide-complete-combinations) covers how common liver-support supplements are typically combined.

## NAC vs Milk Thistle for Fatty Liver

Fatty liver disease (now often called MASLD, or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, which simply means extra fat in the liver linked to weight, blood sugar, and cholesterol) is one of the most common liver problems. Both supplements have been studied for it, with limited results.

- **Milk thistle:** a randomized trial in Malaysia, published in 2017, gave people with fatty liver disease a high dose of silymarin for 48 weeks. It found signs of less scarring in the silymarin group but no clear improvement on the main fatty-liver score the study was designed to measure. Other smaller studies have reported improvements in liver enzymes, but the quality varies.
- **NAC:** has been tested in a handful of small studies in fatty liver, some reporting better liver enzyme numbers. There aren't large, high-quality trials showing it changes how the disease progresses.

Neither supplement replaces what actually moves fatty liver: gradual weight loss if you are overweight, more physical activity, better blood sugar control, and less alcohol. If you've been told you have fatty liver, ask your doctor before starting either one. Our [fatty liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-fatty-liver-supplements) goes through the options in more depth.

## Side Effects and Safety

Both supplements are considered low-risk for most healthy adults at normal doses. Here's what to know about each.

### NAC

- **Stomach upset** is the most common complaint: nausea, heartburn, diarrhea, or vomiting. Taking it with food usually helps.
- **A sulfur or "rotten egg" smell** is normal. NAC contains sulfur.
- **Nitroglycerin and other nitrates.** NAC can strengthen their effect, which may cause bad headaches or a drop in blood pressure. Don't combine them without your doctor's approval.
- **Blood thinners and bleeding.** NAC may slow blood clotting slightly. If you take a blood thinner or have a bleeding disorder, ask first, and stop before surgery as your doctor advises.
- **Asthma.** Breathing problems are mainly a concern with the inhaled form of NAC used in hospitals, but people with asthma should still talk to their doctor before taking it.
- **Activated charcoal** can reduce NAC absorption if taken together.
- **Regulatory status.** In the US, the FDA has gone back and forth on whether NAC can be sold as a dietary supplement, because it was first approved as a drug. It remains widely available, but that history is a reminder that supplement quality and labeling aren't checked the way prescription drugs are.

### Milk thistle

- **Mild digestive effects** such as bloating, gas, or loose stools are the most commonly reported problems.
- **Allergies.** People allergic to plants in the daisy family (ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds, daisies) can react to milk thistle.
- **Blood sugar.** Silymarin may lower blood sugar. If you take diabetes medicine, ask your doctor and watch your numbers.
- **Hormone-sensitive conditions.** Some milk thistle extracts may have weak estrogen-like effects. People with hormone-sensitive conditions are often advised to avoid it.
- **Drug metabolism.** Milk thistle may affect some liver enzymes that process medications. The effects in people appear to be small, but if you take a drug where exact blood levels matter, check with your pharmacist.

### For both

- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding:** there isn't enough safety data. Ask your doctor first.
- **Quality varies.** Supplements aren't tested for purity and dose the way drugs are. Look for brands that use third-party testing.
- **Neither makes heavy drinking safe.** No supplement offsets regular heavy drinking. If you're worried about your liver, a doctor can order a simple blood test.

## How People Typically Take Them

These are general ranges from common product labels and research, not a personal recommendation.

**NAC:** most supplements come in 600 mg capsules. Common use is 600 to 1,200 mg a day, often split into two doses and taken with food to reduce stomach upset. Some people take a dose before going out on the theory that it supports glutathione during drinking. That timing makes biological sense but isn't backed by good human trials.

**Milk thistle:** labels vary a lot, so look at the silymarin content rather than the total weight of the capsule. Many studies used extracts standardized to around 70 to 80 percent silymarin, at roughly 140 mg of silymarin two or three times a day. It's meant to be taken daily over weeks, not just on nights you drink.

## Where DHM Fits In

You might notice that neither NAC nor milk thistle is really a "drinking" supplement. NAC is a glutathione precursor, and milk thistle is a long-term liver herb. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is the one people usually reach for when the goal is the night of drinking itself. It's a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for how it affects alcohol metabolism and the brain's response to alcohol.

To be clear about the evidence: most DHM research comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that reported improvements in some liver markers. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it lets you drink more safely. If you want to see how DHM compares to NAC directly, our [NAC vs DHM guide](/never-hungover/nac-vs-dhm-which-antioxidant-better-liver-protection-2025) walks through it.

If you decide to try DHM, two well-reviewed options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) is worth reading if you take prescription medicine. For a full ranking of liver-support options, including NAC and milk thistle, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

## The Bottom Line

- **NAC** supplies the building block for glutathione, the liver's main antioxidant. Its one proven use is as a hospital antidote for acetaminophen overdose. There is no good evidence that a daily pill protects a healthy drinker's liver or prevents hangovers.
- **Milk thistle** is the most-studied liver herb, gentle and cheap, but the higher-quality trials in alcohol-related liver disease haven't shown clear benefits.
- **Head to head:** NAC has the clearer mechanism; milk thistle has the gentler side-effect profile and the longer history. No study has compared them directly.
- **Together:** there's no known dangerous interaction, but stacking adds side effects and cost without adding proof.
- **What matters more than either:** how much and how often you drink. If you're worried about your liver, ask your doctor for a blood test before reaching for a supplement.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is NAC or milk thistle better for your liver?**

There is no study comparing them head to head. NAC has the clearer mechanism: it supplies cysteine, the building block the liver needs most to make glutathione, and it is the proven hospital antidote for acetaminophen overdose. Milk thistle has been studied longer and tends to be gentler on the stomach, but the higher-quality trials in alcohol-related liver disease have not shown clear benefits. For a healthy social drinker, the honest expectation for either is modest. Talk to your doctor if you have liver concerns.

**Can I take NAC and milk thistle together?**

Generally yes. There is no known dangerous interaction between them, and they often appear together in liver-support formulas. Stacking does make stomach upset more likely and adds a second list of medication cautions to check, so start one at a time and ask your pharmacist if you take prescription medicine.

**Does NAC or milk thistle help with hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that either one prevents or treats hangovers in people. NAC has a plausible theory, because cysteine can react with acetaldehyde and supports glutathione, but that comes from animal and lab studies. Milk thistle has even less support for hangovers. Pacing your drinks, eating, hydrating, and sleeping well matter more.

**Should I take NAC before or after drinking?**

Some people take NAC before drinking on the theory that it supports glutathione while the body processes alcohol, but there are no good human trials showing this timing helps. If you take it, take it with food to reduce stomach upset, stay within the label dose, and check with your doctor if you take nitroglycerin, blood thinners, or other prescription medicine.

**Is milk thistle or NAC better for fatty liver?**

Neither has strong evidence. A 2017 randomized trial of high-dose silymarin in people with fatty liver found signs of less scarring but no clear improvement on its main measure, and NAC has only small studies. Weight loss if needed, more activity, blood sugar control, and less alcohol are what actually improve fatty liver. Ask your doctor before starting either supplement.

**What are the side effects of NAC and milk thistle?**

NAC most often causes nausea, heartburn, diarrhea, and a sulfur smell, and it can interact with nitroglycerin and blood thinners. Milk thistle most often causes mild bloating or loose stools, can trigger reactions in people allergic to ragweed or daisies, and may lower blood sugar. Both lack good safety data in pregnancy.

**Does NAC protect your liver from alcohol?**

NAC helps the liver make glutathione, and in hospitals high-dose NAC protects the liver from acetaminophen poisoning. There is no good evidence that a daily NAC supplement protects a healthy person's liver from alcohol, and it does not make heavy drinking safe. If you're worried about your liver, ask your doctor for a simple blood test.
